The Chilean tinamou (Nothoprocta perdicaria) is a medium-sized ground bird endemic to the agricultural and scrubland habitats of central Chile. Neonates emerge from the egg at a remarkably small body mass of 37.5 grams [Wwb = 37.5 grams], a value that reflects the relatively altricial state of the downy chick despite its precocial capability for immediate mobility. This modest birth weight stands in contrast to the substantial adult morphology the species ultimately attains. Once fully grown, sexually mature individuals reach an ultimate wet weight of 458 grams [Wwi = 458 grams], placing them among the larger representatives of the Tinamidae family. This almost twelve-fold increase in body mass from hatching to adulthood necessitates a prolonged period of intensive growth and nutrient acquisition, a developmental trajectory that is energetically demanding and closely tied to the seasonal availability of seeds and invertebrates in their semi-arid environment.

Under the controlled thermal conditions typical of brooding adults, maintained at the species-specific incubation temperature of 39.45 °C [T = 39.45 °C], the incubation period for the Chilean tinamou lasts approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days], a value that aligns closely with reports for several other tinamou species of similar egg mass. This relatively brief embryonic phase leads to the hatching of highly coordinated chicks that can follow the attending male almost immediately. Field observations corroborate a narrow range for this developmental milestone, with hatching events recorded between 19 and 21 days (19-21 days) [ab = 19-21 days], variation that is often attributed to minor fluctuations in nest microclimate at a temperature of 39.45 °C [T = 39.45 °C]. The precise regulation of nest temperature is critical, as deviations from the optimum can prolong incubation or reduce hatchling viability, underscoring the trade-off between developmental speed and offspring quality in this ground-nesting bird.

Sexual maturation in Nothoprocta perdicaria is a protracted process, with chicks reaching the onset of puberty at 100 days since birth [tp = 100 days since birth] when developing under the stable thermal conditions of 39.45 °C [T = 39.45 °C]. This relatively delayed gonadal development is typical of species that invest heavily in somatic growth before diverting resources toward reproduction, and it ensures that the maturing bird attains a body size and condition sufficient to support the energetic demands of courtship and nesting. The subsequent milestone of first reproduction, signified by the successful initiation of a first brood, occurs noticeably later. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 584 days [tR = approximately 584 days] under the same thermoregulatory regime of 39.45 °C [T = 39.45 °C], meaning that most individuals do not breed until well into their second calendar year. This delayed first breeding is thought to be linked to the competitive dynamics for high-quality nesting territories among males in densely populated habitats.

The fledging period presents another key developmental stage in the life cycle of the Chilean tinamou. Under the species-typical thermoneutral conditions of 39.45 °C [T = 39.45 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 45.75 days [tx = 45.75 days], marking the point at which the young bird achieves sustained flight and nutritional independence from the parental male. This duration is intermediate among the Tinamidae and likely reflects a balance between the need for rapid development to escape ground predators and the slower growth constraints imposed by the chick's initial small size of 37.5 grams [Wwb = 37.5 grams]. The fledgling period culminates in a transition to a fully independent existence, requiring successful foraging on seeds and small arthropods, and it precedes the long juvenile phase leading toward the reproductive stage. The comparatively extended time to independence is a characteristic shared with other species that occupy seasonally variable environments where food resources fluctuate.

Longevity data for the Chilean tinamou indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5,365.5 days [am = approximately 5,365.5 days] in the wild when measured under the prevailing ambient thermal conditions of 39.45 °C [T = 39.45 °C], which equates to nearly 14.7 years. This substantial longevity is unusual for a bird of its body size and is comparable to that of much larger galliform species, suggesting a slow life-history pace with low annual adult mortality. Basal metabolic rate data, obtained from respirometry trials conducted at 33.6 °C [T = 33.6 °C], reveal a resting oxygen consumption of 317.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 317.5 milliliters per hour], a value that falls within the typical range for a 458 gram [Wwi = 458 gram] bird and reflects the energetic costs of maintaining endothermy at moderate temperatures. In terms of reproductive output, females typically produce clutches containing 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 8 eggs per clutch] and can sustain one successful nesting event per year [F_R_i = one successful nesting event per year] under favorable conditions, yielding a modest annual recruitment that is characteristic of a K-selected life-history strategy.
